title: Status page transparency upgrades - taxonomy + templates working session
topics: Customer-facing component taxonomy review (Hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private, plus region scoping)
Naming debate: internal terms (scheduler) vs customer-friendly labels (Capacity & Routing)
Incident update templates walkthrough (investigating/identified/monitoring/resolved) and required fields
Post-incident summary format + SLA and redaction boundaries
Incident-bot / workflow tooling: guided prompts, status page draft sync, approval flow
summary: Cross-functional working session to finalize a customer-facing status page component taxonomy and align on incident communication templates (phase-based updates + cadence language). The group converged on a simpler component naming scheme (avoid internal terms like “scheduler”), agreed on when to use region-level components vs global components, and identified a few edge cases (streaming-only errors, model-family regressions, 429 capacity constraints). Walked through template language for uncertainty and customer actions, plus a lightweight post-incident summary format with a target SLA (Sev1: within 3 business days) while staying within disclosure policy. Tooling questions centered on incident-bot prompts, requiring a next-update time, and a lightweight approval path (SRE lead + Security consulted when needed).

Miles Thornton - Draft incident-bot prompt flow for Investigating/Identified/Monitoring/Resolved + enforce next-update time field - due 2024-06-24
Tomáš Novák - Add mapping guidance section: when to pick region component vs global, and “don’t over-scope” examples - due 2024-06-21
Dr. Aisha Rahman - Provide redaction/disclosure checklist bullets for post-incident summaries (provider issues, exploit-like detail) - due 2024-06-20
Elliot Price - Draft “How to read our status page” outline aligned to taxonomy and templates (customer actions, what we publish) - due 2024-06-25
Dev Patel - Share top 10 support questions during incidents and suggested customer-friendly phrases to reduce back-and-forth - due 2024-06-20
Aisha Bello - Confirm what signals/metrics will back Streaming vs API Gateway components and where gaps exist - due 2024-06-26
next_steps: Talia to schedule 30-min follow-up for final sign-off on taxonomy names + approval workflow
Rafael to pick 1-2 recent incidents and run a “template dry run” to validate the component selection and copy
Miles to propose feature-flag rollout plan for incident-bot changes (pilot one region/service group)
Elliot to coordinate with Docs on placement and wording to avoid overpromising SLA
transcript:
Meeting header
Title: Status page transparency upgrades - taxonomy + templates working session
Date: Tue, Jun 18, 2024
Time: 4:00pm - 4:56pm PT
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Talia Benson, Rafael Mendes, Sean Gallagher, Christine Wong, Miles Thornton, Tomáš Novák, Marissa Cole, Paula Mendes, Dr. Aisha Rahman, Elliot Price, Dev Patel, Aisha Bello

Summary (auto-generated)
- Reviewed status page component taxonomy proposal and naming.
- Walked through incident update templates and cadence guidance.
- Discussed post-incident summary SLA and disclosure boundaries.
- Open questions on incident-bot automation and approvals.

Topics
1) Component taxonomy: Hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private + region scoping
2) Naming and customer comprehension (avoid internal jargon)
3) Template walkthrough: investigating/identified/monitoring/resolved
4) Post-incident summary format, SLA, and redaction
5) Tooling: incident-bot guided prompts, draft sync, approvals

Action items (auto-generated)
- Christine to update taxonomy with examples.
- Miles to draft incident-bot prompt flow.
- Tomáš to add region vs global mapping guidance.
- Aisha (Security) to provide redaction checklist.
- Elliot to draft public doc outline.
- Dev to share top incident support FAQs.
- Aisha (SLO) to confirm signal coverage.

Transcript

[00:00] Talia Benson: Alright, um, thanks everyone for making time. Goal today is to do a working pass on the status page component taxonomy, then walk the update templates end-to-end, and leave with open questions for tooling so Miles can bake it into the incident-bot.

[00:16] Rafael Mendes: Yep. And we should also pin down what we mean by region components. We’ve had like three tickets now where customers are like “which region is broken?” and we’re saying “API degraded” which doesn’t help.

[00:28] Dev Patel: +1. Support basically ends up writing a second status page in Zendesk macros. People ask if it’s streaming-only, if embeddings is down, if it’s us-east only. We don’t have a crisp answer.

[00:40] Sean Gallagher: And we need to make sure whatever we publish is actually backed by signals. If we add ten components and we can’t detect impact, it becomes theater.

[00:51] Aisha Bello: I have notes on signal coverage, but yeah, it’s not like everything has clean SLOs today.

[00:58] Talia Benson: Great. Christine, can you pull up the taxonomy list you drafted?

[01:03] Christine Wong: Yep, one sec. Okay. So top-level we have: “Hosted API”, “Streaming”, “Embeddings”, “Rerank”, “Console”, “Dedicated Control Plane”, “Private Control Plane”, and then “Region-specific Serving” for Hosted API serving by region: us-east, us-west, eu-west.

[01:27] Marissa Cole: Quick gut check: are we putting Console as one component? Because in the past we’ve had issues where rollouts UI is down but inference is fine.

[01:36] Christine Wong: Right now it’s “Console” as one, but we can split into “Console - UI” and “Console - Rollouts” if we think it’s meaningful.

[01:44] Paula Mendes: From product side, I’d prefer we keep it one at first. Customers don’t necessarily know what “Rollouts” means unless they use it a lot. But we can mention in incident updates “Rollouts page failing to load” without making a separate component.

[02:01] Elliot Price: Also docs-wise, fewer components makes the “how to read the status page” page easier. If we split Console too early, it’s more glossary work.

[02:12] Sean Gallagher: I like fewer, but I want “Capacity & Routing” as a component. We keep having partial degradations that aren’t a model crash, it’s like scheduler or routing constraints. If we call it “API” the customer thinks everything is broken.

[02:28] Rafael Mendes: The question is whether we can say “scheduler” publicly. I think no.

[02:32] Sean Gallagher: Yeah, not “scheduler”. “Capacity & Routing” is customer-friendly.

[02:36] Dr. Aisha Rahman: +1 on avoiding internal architecture words. Not for secrecy, just because it invites too many follow-ups. If you say “scheduler” somebody will ask for details, and then we’re in disclosure gray zone.

[02:51] Miles Thornton: From tooling perspective, we can tag incidents with an internal cause like “scheduler” but map to “Capacity & Routing” externally. That’s fine.

[03:02] Christine Wong: So do we add “Capacity & Routing” as its own component alongside “API Gateway”?

[03:07] Rafael Mendes: We don’t have “API Gateway” explicitly yet. We have “Hosted API” which is broad.

[03:12] Sean Gallagher: Right, I think we should break “Hosted API” into “API Gateway” and “Serving”. Otherwise everything goes in “Hosted API”.

[03:19] Aisha Bello: Careful: “Serving” plus region components could get messy. Like if us-east is degraded, do we mark “Serving (us-east)” only, or also mark global “Serving”?

[03:32] Tomáš Novák: That’s exactly what oncall struggles with. People over-select components to be safe, then customers in eu-west are like “are we impacted?” and we can’t answer.

[03:43] Talia Benson: Okay, let’s ground it in an example. The streaming keepalive timeout incident from last month. What components would we have chosen in the new taxonomy?

[03:52] Rafael Mendes: That was streaming-only, mostly. Non-streaming responses were okay.

[03:56] Dev Patel: Yep. Support had a ton of “my stream is cutting off at like 20 seconds” complaints. Standard completion still worked.

[04:03] Christine Wong: So for that we’d select “Streaming” only.

[04:07] Sean Gallagher: Maybe also “Hosted API” if customers see it as “the API”.

[04:11] Tomáš Novák: But that defeats the purpose. The point is to not mark API as broken if only streaming is degraded.

[04:16] Miles Thornton: We can add mapping guidance: if failure is isolated to streaming transport / SSE disconnects, select “Streaming” only, do not also select “API Gateway” unless we have evidence of non-streaming impact.

[04:28] Marissa Cole: That’s good. And in the incident text we can still say “non-streaming requests continue to succeed” so customers can route.

[04:36] Paula Mendes: Also: add customer actions. Like “fall back to non-streaming” or “increase client timeout” if that’s safe.

[04:43] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Just make sure customer actions don’t become “workarounds” that create security issues. But retry/backoff and switching from streaming to non-streaming is fine.

[04:55] Talia Benson: Great. Next example: 429s due to capacity constraints in us-west only.

[05:01] Aisha Bello: That’s a “Capacity & Routing” / “Serving” thing, often with region. We should pick “Serving - us-west” and “Capacity & Routing” maybe.

[05:11] Sean Gallagher: I’d be careful selecting both. If we add too many, again customers can’t interpret.

[05:18] Christine Wong: What if we say “Hosted API Serving (us-west)” and within that component definition, it includes capacity constraints and elevated 429/503.

[05:28] Rafael Mendes: So then what is “Capacity & Routing” for? Only for global routing issues?

[05:33] Sean Gallagher: Or when the capacity issue affects request admission across regions, or model routing decisions, like fallback not working.

[05:41] Miles Thornton: We can encode: if capacity is region-scoped and isolated, choose the region serving component. If the routing layer is misbehaving globally (wrong model variant selection, failover not working), choose “Capacity & Routing”.

[05:55] Tomáš Novák: I can write that as a “if/then” table in the mapping guidelines.

[06:01] Talia Benson: Cool. Let’s list components we’re converging on. Christine, can you read them as you have it, and we adjust live?

[06:09] Christine Wong: Okay. Proposed:
- API Gateway
- Streaming
- Embeddings
- Rerank
- Hosted API Serving - us-east
- Hosted API Serving - us-west
- Hosted API Serving - eu-west
- Capacity & Routing
- Console
- Dedicated Control Plane
- Dedicated Serving (maybe?)
- Private Control Plane

[06:35] Marissa Cole: For Dedicated, do customers want region breakdown? Or is Dedicated per customer anyway.

[06:41] Rafael Mendes: Dedicated is per customer cluster. Publicly we can’t say “Customer X dedicated cluster degraded.” We’d mark “Dedicated” as a product, but then it looks like all dedicated customers are impacted.

[06:55] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Exactly. Don’t put customer-specific details on the public page. Dedicated should be carefully scoped.

[07:03] Sean Gallagher: Maybe on public status page, Dedicated is “Dedicated Control Plane” only. For dedicated serving issues, we do targeted comms via support/CS, not public.

[07:14] Dev Patel: That aligns with what we do today. But customers still want to know if Dedicated is generally unhealthy.

[07:21] Sean Gallagher: If it’s widespread, we can mark “Dedicated Serving” as degraded. If it’s one tenant, we do not.

[07:29] Christine Wong: Then we need criteria for “widespread”. Like “multiple dedicated pools” or “multiple customers”.

[07:36] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Careful with “multiple customers.” You can’t imply customer count in a way that leaks anything sensitive. But “multiple dedicated deployments” might be okay.

[07:45] Paula Mendes: From product, I’d prefer to start with “Dedicated Control Plane” only. Add “Dedicated Serving” later if we have a clear signal and clear rule.

[07:55] Rafael Mendes: Agree. We can treat Dedicated Serving as “out of scope phase 1” and use account-level updates via CSM.

[08:05] Talia Benson: Okay, so phase 1 components: API Gateway, Streaming, Embeddings, Rerank, Hosted Serving by region, Capacity & Routing, Console, Dedicated Control Plane, Private Control Plane.

[08:20] Miles Thornton: That’s nine-ish plus the region components.

[08:24] Aisha Bello: We should validate that we can instrument each of those. I’m pretty confident on API Gateway and streaming disconnects. Embeddings and rerank we can track per-route. Capacity & Routing is trickier.

[08:38] Sean Gallagher: Capacity & Routing could be defined by elevated 429/503 where gateway is fine but admissions fail, plus increased latency from queueing. We can build a composite signal.

[08:51] Aisha Bello: That’s doable but not by next week.

[08:55] Talia Benson: That’s okay, we can roll out components with a “signals in progress” note internally, but we should not publish a component that oncall can’t reliably select.

[09:06] Christine Wong: Totally. We can keep it in taxonomy but maybe hide it from the public page until the dashboard is ready.

[09:13] Miles Thornton: Statuspage lets us create components but keep them in a “not visible” state? I think so. Or we can just not create it yet.

[09:22] Sean Gallagher: Let’s not create zombie components. If it’s not used, it confuses.

[09:26] Talia Benson: Cool. Next: templates. I want to walk through the four phases: Investigating, Identified, Monitoring, Resolved. And specifically: what we require in each, what we ban (like over-specific provider blame), and update cadence.

[09:44] Paula Mendes: Also wording consistency, like “degraded performance” vs “partial outage”. Customers read those literally.

[09:51] Rafael Mendes: We have internal severity definitions. We need a mapping to customer language.

[09:55] Tomáš Novák: I’ve got a draft mapping: Sev2 might still be “degraded performance” if it’s partial, but Sev1 should often be “partial outage” if requests are failing.

[10:06] Sean Gallagher: SLO burn matters too. But we can keep it simple for oncall.

[10:12] Talia Benson: I’ll read the Investigating template first. It’s basically: “We’re investigating reports of X. Impact: who/what is affected. Mitigation: what customers can do (retry/backoff, fallback model, switch region). Next update by: time.”

[10:27] Elliot Price: For docs, we should standardize the “Next update” phrasing. Like “Next update within 30 minutes.”

[10:33] Miles Thornton: For incident-bot, we can enforce a required “next update time” field that goes into the status post.

[10:38] Rafael Mendes: That would help. We often forget and then it looks like we disappeared.

[10:43] Dev Patel: Support gets hammered when there’s no next update. People assume we’re not working it.

[10:49] Dr. Aisha Rahman: One thing: in Investigating, avoid stating a cause. Don’t say “AWS outage” unless confirmed. Use “upstream provider” at most, and even that is risky.

[11:02] Sean Gallagher: Yes, “we’re investigating elevated 5xx” is fine.

[11:06] Marissa Cole: For customer actions: can we say “use a fallback model”? That’s a product promise question.

[11:12] Paula Mendes: We can say “if you have configured fallbacks” or “consider switching to a compatible model variant” without promising it will work.

[11:20] Rafael Mendes: And we can link docs on fallback policies once Elliot publishes.

[11:25] Elliot Price: Yep. And we can say “if you’re using the Redwood SDK, enable automatic retry with exponential backoff.”

[11:33] Miles Thornton: Incident-bot could include suggested bullet list of actions based on selected component: streaming vs embeddings etc.

[11:41] Talia Benson: Let’s move to Identified template. This is the one people misuse. It’s when we have high confidence in the cause or at least the failing subsystem and we have mitigation underway.

[11:52] Tomáš Novák: Oncall tends to jump to Identified too fast because it feels better.

[11:57] Sean Gallagher: Right. If we’re not sure, stay Investigating.

[12:00] Christine Wong: The Identified template I have: “We’ve identified the cause as [customer-safe category] and are applying mitigation. Impact: … Mitigation: … Next update by …”

[12:12] Dr. Aisha Rahman: The bracket “customer-safe category” is important. For example: “a configuration change affecting streaming connections” is okay. “A vulnerability in X library” is not.

[12:26] Rafael Mendes: We also need to define approved root cause categories. Like “capacity constraints”, “network instability”, “deploy regression”, “upstream provider issue”.

[12:36] Sean Gallagher: Agree. But keep it not too detailed.

[12:39] Aisha Bello: And for metrics, categories are useful for trend tracking.

[12:45] Talia Benson: Monitoring template: “Mitigation applied, we’re seeing recovery, continuing to monitor.” Resolved: “Issue resolved, all systems operational.” Then post-incident summary follow-up.

[12:58] Dev Patel: Can we set expectations that post-incident summary comes within X days? Enterprise customers ask.

[13:05] Paula Mendes: We can say: “We’ll publish a summary for significant incidents.” But then define “significant.”

[13:12] Rafael Mendes: Proposal is Sev1 and Sev0 get a customer-facing post-incident summary within 3 business days.

[13:19] Sean Gallagher: And Sev2 maybe optional.

[13:21] Dr. Aisha Rahman: I’m okay with 3 business days as a target, but we should not make it a hard public SLA unless we can hit it.

[13:29] Talia Benson: Internally we can call it an SLA. Externally we can call it “typically within 3 business days.”

[13:36] Elliot Price: Wording matters. We can say “We aim to publish within 3 business days for major incidents.”

[13:44] Dev Patel: That’s fine. It gives support something to point at.

[13:49] Miles Thornton: Tooling can help. We can auto-create a summary doc stub and send reminders.

[13:56] Talia Benson: Let’s talk post-incident summary template. I’m thinking sections: Impact, Timeline (start, detection, mitigation, resolution), Root cause category, What we did during incident, Prevention/next steps.

[14:12] Sean Gallagher: That matches internal postmortems but less detail.

[14:15] Dr. Aisha Rahman: And include a redaction checklist: remove customer names, remove internal hostnames, remove exploit-like steps, avoid attributing blame to providers unless public.

[14:27] Rafael Mendes: Sometimes provider issues are obvious. Like if it’s a cloud region outage.

[14:32] Dr. Aisha Rahman: You can say “an upstream cloud provider network event” without naming vendor, unless vendor published it.

[14:39] Christine Wong: That’s going to be annoying for customers who just want to know if it’s “AWS.”

[14:43] Sean Gallagher: Yeah but we’re not going to get into contractual or finger-pointing.

[14:49] Talia Benson: Okay. Open tooling questions. Miles, what do you need from us to build the guided prompts?

[14:57] Miles Thornton: Two things: 1) the canonical component list and names, and 2) the required fields per update stage. For example, require “impact” + “next update” always, and at least one of “mitigation” or “what we know.”

[15:15] Tomáš Novák: Also we should block empty updates. People do “Investigating” with zero content just to start the clock.

[15:22] Rafael Mendes: Yeah, like “We are investigating.” Period.

[15:25] Miles Thornton: We can add guardrails: prevent publishing if it doesn’t include impact OR mitigation OR next update time. But we said next update time should be required anyway.

[15:37] Sean Gallagher: I’d say require impact and next update time. Mitigation may be unknown early.

[15:42] Paula Mendes: Agree. It’s okay to say “no workaround yet” as long as the customer knows what’s affected.

[15:48] Dev Patel: Impact should be specific: “streaming responses may disconnect” not “API issues.”

[15:55] Elliot Price: We should give “impact phrase examples” per component.

[16:01] Christine Wong: I can add examples to taxonomy definitions.

[16:05] Talia Benson: Approval workflow. Who can publish? Rafael, do you want it to be incident commander only, or oncall SRE?

[16:14] Rafael Mendes: Practically, oncall SRE does it. Incident commander sometimes is same person, sometimes not.

[16:20] Sean Gallagher: For Sev1+, we can require SRE lead review in Slack before publishing, but not block on it. We need speed.

[16:29] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Security should be “consulted” when there’s suspected security incident or when wording touches vulnerabilities or customer data. Not every outage.

[16:40] Miles Thornton: We can implement: by default, publish rights for oncall SRE and incident commander. For certain incident labels (security_possible=true), require explicit approver in the workflow.

[16:54] Paula Mendes: Is that label reliable? Because people forget to set it.

[16:58] Sean Gallagher: We can also trigger Security review when component “Private Control Plane” is selected, maybe? Since that touches regulated customers.

[17:06] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Not necessarily. Private control plane incidents can be normal outages. But yes, it’s higher sensitivity.

[17:13] Talia Benson: Let’s capture: “Security consult if security suspected or if the draft includes sensitive root cause details.” We’ll write a policy doc.

[17:25] Tomáš Novák: Runbook should say: if unsure, ping #eng-security and paste the draft.

[17:31] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Yep.

[17:33] (crosstalk)

[17:34] Aisha Bello: Can I jump back to region scoping? I think we need a crisp rule: If impact is isolated to a region and customers can route elsewhere, we should always mark the region component, not the global one.

[17:46] Rafael Mendes: Agree, but sometimes we don’t know region quickly.

[17:49] Aisha Bello: Then in Investigating, we can say “We are investigating reports primarily in us-west” with uncertainty language.

[17:56] Christine Wong: Yeah, template should allow “we believe impact is primarily…”

[18:00] Sean Gallagher: Uncertainty language is important. Like “We’re still determining scope.”

[18:05] Talia Benson: Let’s do a quick pass on uncertainty phrases we like.

[18:09] Paula Mendes: “We’re investigating and will provide scope as soon as we confirm.”

[18:13] Dev Patel: “Some customers may experience…” is useful.

[18:17] Elliot Price: But avoid “all customers”. Unless sure.

[18:20] Rafael Mendes: I like “A subset of requests” or “a subset of customers in region X.”

[18:26] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Avoid quantifying. Don’t say “10%”. That’s usually wrong and becomes discoverable.

[18:32] Sean Gallagher: Yep.

[18:35] Talia Benson: Okay. Back to templates: update cadence. I’m proposing: Sev0/Sev1 update every 30 minutes, or at least with a next update time. Sev2 hourly. Sev3 at discretion.

[18:49] Rafael Mendes: 30 minutes is aggressive if the incident is stable but long.

[18:54] Tomáš Novák: But if we enforce next-update time, we can say “next update in 60 minutes” when nothing changes.

[19:02] Dev Patel: Customers just want to know you’re still on it.

[19:06] Marissa Cole: Also the content quality matters more than frequency. But we can keep it simple.

[19:12] Miles Thornton: Tool can remind you when next update is overdue.

[19:16] Talia Benson: Great. Now open question: do we show components like “Embeddings” and “Rerank” publicly? Some customers don’t use them.

[19:25] Paula Mendes: But the customers who do use them really care. And it addresses the “what’s impacted?” problem.

[19:31] Sean Gallagher: It’s fine. The status page can have components that some customers ignore.

[19:35] Elliot Price: We just need glossary entries for each.

[19:38] Christine Wong: I’ll write short definitions: “Embeddings API: vector embedding requests; does not affect chat completion.” Similar for rerank.

[19:48] Aisha Bello: Also note that “Embeddings” and “Rerank” are routes on the same gateway, so API Gateway can still be healthy while those routes fail due to backend.

[20:02] Rafael Mendes: Exactly why we split.

[20:05] Talia Benson: Okay. Let’s talk about the “API Gateway” component itself. What constitutes gateway degradation?

[20:12] Aisha Bello: Elevated 5xx at the edge, auth failures, request timeouts before hitting model serving. Also widespread 401 due to auth service.

[20:23] Sean Gallagher: And “Serving” by region covers model runtime failures, high latency, capacity 429s in a region.

[20:31] Miles Thornton: From mapping perspective, we’ll need a decision tree oncall can follow: is it transport/streaming, is it route-specific, is it region-specific serving, is it gateway.

[20:42] Tomáš Novák: I’ll draft a runbook page with scenarios: “Streaming disconnects”, “Embeddings latency only”, “429 in us-west”, “Console UI down”, “Private deploy control plane unreachable.”

[20:55] Dev Patel: Include “model-family specific” issues too. Like “Llama-3 only is failing.” Customers ask if they can switch models.

[21:03] Rafael Mendes: That’s a big one. Do we make “Model catalog” components? I’d prefer no.

[21:08] Paula Mendes: Same. Too granular.

[21:11] Sean Gallagher: We can handle it in incident text: “Impacts requests to Model X and compatible variants.” But components remain route-level.

[21:21] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Be careful naming specific models if it reveals something sensitive. But generally model names are public.

[21:28] Elliot Price: And in docs we can say “If you are pinned to a specific model version, consider switching to a compatible version.”

[21:35] Christine Wong: We need a consistent phrase for that.

[21:38] Talia Benson: Okay. Switching gears: post-incident summary. Do we want to publish them on status page incident page, or separate blog-like page?

[21:48] Elliot Price: Best is a link from the incident page. Some status page providers allow “postmortem” link.

[21:55] Miles Thornton: We can attach a link to a doc or to docs site.

[22:01] Paula Mendes: Docs site is better long term.

[22:04] Sean Gallagher: But we need it to be low friction. If it requires a docs PR every time, we’ll miss SLA.

[22:11] Elliot Price: We can do a lightweight markdown template that’s published via a simple workflow. Maybe not full docs pipeline, but still reviewed.

[22:20] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Review is key. At least for Sev0/Security-ish events.

[22:26] Rafael Mendes: Maybe the workflow is: auto-create stub in Confluence, then we copy a sanitized version to status page.

[22:34] Talia Benson: Let’s not over-design. For now: the summary is a section on the incident page, posted after resolution, within 3 business days.

[22:44] Miles Thornton: That’s easiest. We can add a “post-incident summary” field in incident-bot that posts to status page.

[22:50] Christine Wong: Does Statuspage support a “Postmortem” update type? I think yes.

[22:55] Sean Gallagher: Even if not, we can post a normal update with summary.

[23:00] Dev Patel: Support would love a permalink.

[23:04] Talia Benson: Noted. Now, I want to capture open questions list:
1) Do we add Capacity & Routing component in phase 1, or wait for signals?
2) Dedicated serving: do we keep out of public page for now?
3) Approval policy: for Sev1+ do we require review or just recommended?
4) Post-incident summary: exact location and minimal review required.

[23:25] Sean Gallagher: On (1), I’d wait until Aisha confirms signals.

[23:28] Aisha Bello: Yep, I can confirm by next week.

[23:31] Paula Mendes: On (2) I vote: keep dedicated serving out.

[23:34] Rafael Mendes: Same.

[23:36] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Same.

[23:38] Talia Benson: Great. On (3), Rafael?

[23:41] Rafael Mendes: Recommended review. Not hard gate. But the bot can post a Slack message “paste your draft here for review” to #incidents-comms.

[23:50] Miles Thornton: That’s easy. We can prompt: “Request review? y/n” and it posts the draft.

[23:55] Sean Gallagher: Love it.

[23:57] Talia Benson: On (4), summary review: maybe SRE lead signs off, Security if needed.

[24:04] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Yes.

[24:06] Elliot Price: And we should ensure the tone is consistent. Not too defensive, not too detailed.

[24:12] Marissa Cole: One more thing on templates: make sure we don’t promise credits or compensation in status posts.

[24:18] Paula Mendes: Good call. That’s support/CS contract-specific.

[24:22] Dev Patel: Yep. People ask, but we handle separately.

[24:26] Talia Benson: Great catch. Add to “do not include” list.

[24:31] (brief silence)

[24:33] Miles Thornton: Can we talk about the “draft sync” idea? I want to auto-create a status update draft when the incident moves to Investigating in PagerDuty.

[24:42] Rafael Mendes: That would be huge.

[24:44] Tomáš Novák: But it could create noise if incidents are false alarms.

[24:48] Sean Gallagher: Maybe only for Sev1+ or when an incident is declared.

[24:52] Miles Thornton: Exactly. Trigger on “incident declared” event, not just any page.

[24:57] Aisha Bello: Also: include selected components in the incident metadata so we can track component frequency.

[25:03] Miles Thornton: Yup, we can add a status_component tag.

[25:06] Talia Benson: Keep going.

[25:08] Miles Thornton: Flow would be:
- Incident declared (Sev and initial hypothesis)
- Bot prompts: choose components (with guidance)
- Bot generates Investigating draft with placeholders
- Oncall edits and publishes
